title: The Curse Of Good Intentions
text:
The Curse Of Good Intentions

Udith Sikand

Gavekal Research | 13 Oct 2026

The Reserve Bank of India’s increasingly heavy-handed efforts to defend the rupee risk doing more harm than good. By imposing administrative curbs on currency hedging, the central bank may deter the very foreign capital inflows needed to ease depreciation pressures. It is the sort of policy predicament that the economist Lant Pritchett had in mind when he dubbed India a “flailing state” where limited state capacity often frustrates even well-intentioned policies.The Indian rupee has been sliding since mid-2025, with its decline accelerating after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March sent oil prices soaring. Pressured by higher fuel prices, foreign capital outflows and rising global interest rates, the rupee has been one of Asia’s weakest currencies this year, falling -5.5% against the US dollar. To stem the sell-off, the RBI launched a special scheme in early June to attract US dollars from wealthy expatriate Indians, generating inflows of US$130bn over the summer. Against an expected current account deficit of around US$80bn in 2026 and equity portfolio outflows of around US$30bn, it seemed the worst was over for the currency (see India’s Hawkish Turn).
